findings.title: Custom grant shortcuts are not constrained to the fixed two-character token format
findings.body: The encoder format unconditionally writes the grant shortcut, while `getTokenContextFromTokenId` requires the entire context prefix to be exactly six characters and slices the grant shortcut as exactly characters 4-5. `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory.getShortcut()` neither enforces nor documents a two-character requirement (its Javadoc even says it is usually a three-letter shortcut). Consequently, an extension implementing a valid-looking shortcut such as `custom`/`abc` can issue access tokens successfully, but those token IDs cannot subsequently be decoded and will throw `IllegalArgumentException`. Validate shortcut length and uniqueness during factory initialization (and dynamic refresh), or make the format length-delimited.

findings.title: Access-token event matcher does not validate the expected grant shortcut
findings.body: `isAccessTokenId` checks `substring(3, 5)`, although the two-character grant portion of the documented six-character prefix starts at zero-based offset 4. It also returns false when that substring equals the expected shortcut, rather than when it differs. For normal IDs such as `onrtac:<uuid>`, the extracted value is `ta`, so every expected shortcut is accepted as long as the suffix is a UUID. The updated integration assertions therefore cannot detect a missing or incorrect grant-type encoding; compare `substring(4, 6)` and reject when it is not equal to `expectedGrantShortcut`.

findings.title: Raw token ID is not null-checked despite the constructor contract
findings.body: The final null check repeats `grantType` while using the error message for `rawTokenId`, so `rawTokenId` may be null. `encodeTokenId` then silently concatenates it as the literal string `null`, producing a syntactically valid encoded ID that decodes to a different raw ID instead of failing fast. Check `rawTokenId` here to preserve token-ID integrity for SPI callers.
